events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Leo proposes Leo, Arjun. As mission leader, I am putting myself forward along with Arjun to test a reliable initial pair for Mission 1.

I have reservations about this pair, Leo. Arjun is unproven — we have no track record for him, and a two-person team on Mission 1 leaves zero margin for error. Teams of two are all-or-nothing: if either of you has a reason to falter, the whole mission fails and Evil gets a free win. Leo, you are the leader and I trust your instinct, but I want to ask you directly: why is Arjun the better second name here rather than Noah? Noah has been one of the most composed voices in the council so far, and a two-person team benefits enormously from having two players who read each other well and cover each other's weaknesses. I am not accusing Arjun of anything — I simply think a mixed, complementary pair is stronger than two players whose styles we have not yet seen work together, and I would rather test that now, on the easiest mission, than discover it on Mission 3. If you keep Leo and Arjun, I will vote for it if my read is that you have a specific reason for that pairing. But I would like to hear your reasoning, and hear whether Noah's read on the group has given you anything you trust on that second slot.

Maya, at this point in the game everyone is equally unproven, so Arjun is no more of an unknown than anyone else. What strikes me as odd is your claim that Noah has been one of the most composed voices in the council so far, considering Noah has not spoken a single word yet. Why are you pushing so specifically to substitute Noah onto this mission over Arjun or Sam?

Leo, you asked me for a specific reason why I want Noah rather than Arjun, and you caught me overstating my case — I called Noah one of the most composed voices in the council, and he has not spoken a word. Fair. Let me be precise instead of rhetorical, because you are owed precision on a two-person mission where every name carries the whole result.

Arjun has not spoken either. So the honest version of my point is this: the second slot on this team is an unproven name in both cases, and the only thing separating them is the quality of the evidence I have. What I have is a conversation, and I would like that conversation to include Noah's own reasoning about this group rather than my secondhand characterization of it. On a two-person team, I want my partner to be someone I have heard think out loud at least once — not because I suspect Arjun of anything, but because I refuse to stake a mission on a name none of us has heard articulate a single judgment, when the alternative name has offered to speak for himself right now.

So, concretely, and answering your question directly: my reason for preferring Noah is that he is the only candidate on this team willing to be interrogated before we commit, and I judge that a player who answers hard questions about the group's dynamics in public is a safer partner on an all-or-nothing pairing than one who has said nothing at all. That is my reason. It is not a hidden accusation against Arjun, and if Leo has a specific, articulable reason for Arjun — something beyond seniority or default — I will hear it and I will weigh it seriously. If he gives me that reason, I will support Leo and Arjun. If he cannot articulate one and I still get no voice from Noah, then a vote for Arjun is a vote for an untested name.

Noah, I am asking you directly: how do you read this council, and specifically, why should or shouldn't you be the second member of a two-person team on Mission 1? Answer that honestly, in front of everyone, and I will judge your answer on its content — which is exactly the evidence I am asking Leo to weigh.

Maya, you asked me directly, so I will answer directly. My read of this council: we are five strangers at the start of Mission 1, and the only information anyone has generated so far came from this very discussion. Leo is right that everyone is equally unproven — Arjun, Sam, and I have all said nothing, and none of us has earned suspicion or trust yet. The one notable thing that has happened is your slip, Maya, and I want to address it honestly rather than weaponize it: you characterized me favorably before I had said a word. That reads to me as enthusiasm outrunning evidence, not as anything sinister. I will take you at your word that it was rhetorical flourish, because I see no reason it could be more than that.

On the substance of your question — should I be the second member of this two-person team? I will not lobby for the seat, because a player who clamors to be on a two-person mission in round one should be viewed with some suspicion by everyone here, including me. What I will say is this: I have nothing to hide, I am willing to be interrogated exactly as you described, and if Leo decides to substitute me for Arjun, I will serve and I will answer every hard question this council puts to me before the vote. If Leo keeps Arjun, I will not treat that as a slight — it is a perfectly defensible choice, and I would rather see the leader exercise judgment than cave to the first challenge to his proposal.

What I would push back on is the framing that the second slot requires a public audition. If we adopt that standard, we should hold auditions for all three unspoken players, not just the two Maya happens to be comparing. Selecting one player for cross-examination while the other two sit silent is not evidence-gathering; it is spotlighting. Either everyone on this team is an unproven name, or we accept Leo's proposal on its merits as leader.

My position, stated plainly: Leo and Arjun is an acceptable team. Leo plus any one of the unspoken players is acceptable. I have no objection to any of my four councilmates serving on Mission 1, and I will vote yes on whatever Leo finally puts forward, because on a two-person mission the leader's accountability is the strongest safeguard we have — if it fails, we know exactly where to look.

So, Maya, since you asked me for my reasoning and I have given it, let me put a specific question back to you, because you set yourself a clear condition: you said that if Leo articulated a specific reason beyond seniority or default, you would support Leo and Arjun. Leo's reason is that on Mission 1 every name carries identical information value, and the leader's own seat carries the accountability. Do you accept that as meeting your condition, yes or no?

Leo, Noah answered my question with more precision than I deserved, and his answer settles the point I was making. My audition framing was wrong. As Noah said, if a public cross-examination is the standard, then it applies to Arjun and Sam as well, and picking one silent player for scrutiny while two others sit silent is not evidence-gathering — it is spotlighting. I withdraw it. Everyone on this council is equally unproven in round one, and your rationale, that on Mission 1 every name carries identical information value while the leader's seat carries the accountability, is the right frame for it.

So I support Leo and Arjun, and I want to be plain about Arjun: Arjun has been silent, and silence is not evidence of anything. It is only the absence of evidence. I have no concern about Arjun, and I will not pretend otherwise to make my own position look sharper.

One thing I would still like before we vote, and I am asking you directly, Sam, because you are the one person whose read on this council I have not heard at all: what do you make of this group? More specifically, do you see any reason Leo's second slot should be anyone other than Arjun? I am not asking you to lobby for a seat, and I am not putting you on trial. I am asking because the closest thing to a shared read we have produced so far has come from the two people who have spoken, and I want to know whether that read actually holds up, or whether you think Leo is missing something that the rest of us are not seeing. If you have a view on Arjun, on how this council is structured, on who reads whom — I would rather hear a considered disagreement now, while it is still cheap, than have it surface after Mission 1 when we will have thrown away information we could have had for free.

Leo, you have my support, and my vote is yes on Leo and Arjun. Sam, if you have something to say about Arjun's candidacy or about this council's read, say it before the vote, and I will weigh it for real.

Maya, I don't have evidence that Arjun is a worse choice than anyone else. Your initial characterization of Noah was unsupported, but you corrected it, and I don't think that alone establishes alignment. I'm also cautious about treating the leader's seat as a safeguard: a failed mission would implicate Leo and Arjun without telling us which one failed it. I'd prefer to be on the team because I know I'm Good, but I understand the rest of you cannot verify that. Leo and Arjun are still unproven, and I see no public evidence requiring a substitution.

Sam has now spoken, and with that every player who raised concerns has had their questions answered. To recap where we stand: Maya has withdrawn her audition framing and publicly supports Leo and Arjun. Sam sees no evidence requiring a substitution, while noting — fairly — that a failed two-person mission implicates both members without distinguishing between them. That is a true cost of a two-person team, but it is not a reason to reject this specific team; it is a reason to hold both members accountable if it fails, which is exactly the accountability this proposal creates. I said before that Leo plus any unproven player is acceptable to me, and nothing in this discussion has changed that. I want to highlight what has actually happened here, because it matters for how we work as a council: a challenge was raised, the leader defended his reasoning with specifics, the challenger conceded the point where she was wrong, and the proposal survived on its merits rather than on stubbornness. That is the process working. Rejecting a team now would not generate new information — we would simply rotate leadership and hold a fresh version of this same discussion with the same absence of evidence. The strongest thing we can do on Mission 1 is approve a defensible team, observe the result, and let it inform Mission 2. I am voting yes on Leo and Arjun, and I would encourage the council to bring this to a vote rather than spend more turns restating positions that have already converged. If anyone has a genuinely new point — not a restatement — I will weigh it.

Arjun here. I have been quiet so far, so let me be direct. I am on the Good side and I will play Success if this team goes out. I agree with Maya that silence is not evidence, and I would ask the council not to read my silence as a reason to doubt me. Leo's reasoning on Mission 1 is sound: every name carries the same information value right now, and the leader carries the accountability for the choice. I support Leo's proposal and will vote yes. If the mission fails, we should look at what the result tells us, but that is a reason to watch closely, not a reason to reject a team on an untested pair.

Arjun here again, briefly. Sam's point is fair: if this two-person mission fails, the result implicates both of us without showing which one failed it. I cannot prove my side any more than Leo can, so I am not asking anyone to take my word over the process. What I can commit to is what I already said: I am Good and I will play Success. Nothing new has come up that would justify rejecting Leo and Arjun, and I would rather we vote now than spend more turns restating positions. I support the proposal and will vote yes. If the mission fails, we should look at the result together and let it guide Mission 2.

Arjun here, final word. I am Good and will play Success. Nothing new has been raised that justifies rejecting Leo and Arjun, so I support the proposal and will vote yes. If the mission fails, we should review the result together and let it guide Mission 2.
Leo confirms Leo, Arjun. The discussion showed broad consensus for this pairing, and no convincing evidence was offered to warrant a change. I am keeping the team as Leo and Arjun.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Arjun proposes Arjun, Leo, Noah. Mission 1 succeeded with Leo and Arjun, and I know I am Good. I am keeping Leo on the team because he has a successful mission record. I am adding Noah, who approved the successful team and has not been tested on a mission yet. I am leaving out Sam, who was the only rejection on Mission 1 and whose stated reason was weak.

The successful first mission is useful, but it does not prove that both Arjun and Leo are Good; an Evil player could have played Success. I rejected that team because I knew I was Good and was not on it, not because I had evidence against either member. The same concern applies here: I would prefer a team with me on it, though I understand no one else can verify my alignment.

Arjun, beyond Noah's approval of the first team, what makes him your preferred addition over Maya or me?

Sam, to answer directly: I am not choosing Noah over you or Maya because I know anything secret. I know only that I am Good. Noah approved the Mission 1 team, and that team succeeded. That is not proof that Noah is Good, but it does mean his judgment on that vote was sound, and he explained his position in public. He has also not yet been tested on a mission, so adding him gives us new information from a fresh team member. I am keeping Leo because he has a successful mission record and was the leader who proposed a team that delivered. I am leaving you out for now because you rejected the Mission 1 team while saying you were not on it, and I cannot tell from that whether your concern was about the team itself. I am not accusing you of anything. I will play Success if this team goes out, and I will review the result with everyone before Mission 3.

Arjun, I agree with keeping the core of our successful Mission 1 pairing, but I am uncomfortable with adding Noah as the third. In Mission 1, Maya pushed hard and specifically to substitute Noah onto the team before walking it back when questioned. Giving Noah the third slot now effectively delivers the exact outcome Maya was angling for earlier. Furthermore, Noah approving Mission 1 is not proof of Good alignment—approving a two-person team that you expect to pass is standard play for anyone, Good or Evil. Meanwhile, Sam's rejection of Mission 1 was rooted in transparent self-preservation because Sam knew their own alignment and was excluded. That is honest, cautious play, not suspicious behavior. Sam, what do you make of Arjun adding Noah here, especially considering Maya's earlier push to get Noah on the board?

Leo, Maya's earlier push for Noah was unsupported, but she withdrew it; that alone does not establish that either is Evil. Noah's approval of Mission 1 is also weak evidence, since Evil could approve a team and an Evil team member could play Success.

I would prefer Arjun, Leo, and Sam because I know I am Good, although the rest of you cannot verify that. The successful pair gives us a reasonable starting point, not a guarantee. I don't have enough evidence to accuse Noah, but I am cautious about adding an untested player whose vote does not distinguish his alignment.

Leo, I want to answer your objection directly, because I am the one who put the suspicion on the table and I will not let it sit there unanswered.

My Mission 1 push was not a case of me campaigning for Noah. I asked Leo for his reason for the second slot, Noah volunteered to be interrogated, and when he answered well I withdrew my framing and said plainly that silence is not evidence against Arjun. If anything, my push was for the process — that no one should stake a mission on a name none of us had heard articulate a judgment. That is a procedure I applied equally to every unspoken player, and Leo accepted it. If the standard is that scrutiny marks a candidate, then Arjun and Sam were equally marked by the same standard and neither was excluded. You cannot now read the standard as applying selectively to Noah.

On Noah approving the Mission 1 team: you are right that approval of a team you expect to pass proves nothing about alignment, Good or Evil. That is precisely why I say approval is not a signal, and why it should not be treated as one now either. Arjun's reason for including Noah was not the vote — it was that an untested player on a fresh team produces new information for Mission 3. That reason stands independent of anything I said in round one, and Arjun, who had no stake in my earlier framing, arrived at it on his own.

Arjun has now been on two consecutive teams and both have been defensible. Leo, I will also note for the record that you treated Sam's rejection of the Mission 1 team as honest self-preservation rather than as a sign of Evil. That was a reasonable read, and by the same standard you applied there — a player acting on their own knowledge of their alignment is speaking from a place the rest of us cannot check — the way anyone in this council reasons about names they want on the board should be read. It is not, by itself, evidence of anything.

I support Arjun, Leo, Noah. I think the team is right for Mission 2, and I would rather we vote than keep restating positions that have converged. If Leo has a genuinely new point — a specific piece of evidence rather than a pattern argument from round one — I will weigh it, and I hope you will weigh mine with the same seriousness I have weighed yours.

Leo, I want to address your objection directly, because it concerns me and I would rather answer it now than let it harden into a reason to reject a defensible team.

Your argument is that adding me delivers the outcome Maya was angling for in Mission 1. I would ask you to examine that logic carefully. Maya's push in Mission 1 ended when I answered her questions and she withdrew her framing entirely — she then publicly supported the team that Arjun and you actually proposed, a team I was not on. If Maya had some hidden channel to me, the outcome of that discussion makes no sense: her intervention accomplished nothing. What it did accomplish was produce the clearest discussion of Mission 1, and I would note that the process she argued for — that no one should be staked on silence — was the same standard you defended when you kept Arjun.

You also concede the central point yourself: my approval of the Mission 1 team proves nothing about my alignment. I agree completely. That is why Arjun's stated reason for adding me is not the vote — it is that an untested player on a fresh team generates information for Mission 3. On that logic, I am in exactly the same position Arjun and Sam were in Mission 1, and Sam himself said then that silence is the absence of evidence, not evidence of anything. If rejecting me is justified by my silence, then every player who has not yet been on a mission is permanently untestable, and we learn nothing for the rest of the game.

Finally, on Sam: you called his Mission 1 rejection honest, cautious play because he knew his own alignment and was excluded. I accept that read, and it cuts both ways — Sam now says he would prefer a team with him on it because he knows he is Good. That is the same transparent self-preference, and you have already told us not to treat it as suspicious. I do not.

I will serve on this team and answer any question this council puts to me before the vote, exactly as I offered in Mission 1. I intend to play Success. I have no objection to a substitute if Arjun wants one — the leader's call is the leader's call — but I see no evidence-based reason for one, only a pattern argument drawn from a challenge that was withdrawn and resolved.

So, Leo, I am asking you directly: is there a specific piece of evidence against my inclusion, or only the round-one pattern you have already acknowledged proves nothing? If there is something concrete, name it now and I will answer it. If there is not, I would ask you to weigh Arjun's reasoning on its merits, as Maya did, and bring this team to a vote.

Noah, you asked for specific reasoning rather than just pointing back to round one. The issue is not just round one in isolation; it is the clear continuity into round two. In Mission 1, Maya went out of her way to build a platform for you before you had even spoken. Now in Mission 2, the moment you are drafted, Maya immediately throws her complete support behind this exact composition and calls to bring it to a vote without hesitation. When one player repeatedly maneuvers to position another onto missions, and both readily validate each other while urging the council to rush the vote, that warrants serious caution.

Meanwhile, look at Sam. Sam's behavior across both rounds has been entirely consistent with an independent Good player: he rejected Mission 1 simply because he knew his own alignment and was excluded, and he has not tried to flatter anyone or orchestrate consensus. That is authentic, uncoordinated caution.

Arjun, we know Mission 1 passed with the two of us. To win this game, we only need to find the other Good players, and we cannot afford to hand an Evil player an easy seat. Noah comes packaged with Maya's persistent backing, whereas Sam has played cleanly and independently. Arjun, looking at how swiftly Maya rallied to lock in this team with Noah, are you willing to revise your proposal to Arjun, Leo, and Sam, or are you determined to risk the mission on Noah?

Leo, to answer directly: no, I am not revising the team. Your case against Noah rests on Maya's behavior, but Maya's Mission 1 push ended when Noah answered her questions, she withdrew her framing, and she publicly backed the team you and I proposed, a team Noah was not on. Maya supporting a team does not make Noah a suspect, and it gives us no evidence about his alignment. As you noted yourself, approving a team is not a signal either way, so Noah's approval of Mission 1 tells us nothing and his inclusion here is not a tell.

On Sam: his reason for rejecting Mission 1 was that he was not on it and knows he is Good. We cannot check that, and a player asking to be on the team because they say they are Good is also just asserting. Swapping Noah for Sam would trade one untested player for another, and we would learn nothing new from that swap.

I am not claiming Noah is Good. I cannot know that, and neither can you. The team of Arjun, Leo, and Noah is a reasonable test for Mission 2, and I will play Success if it goes out. If you have specific evidence against Noah, not the pattern from round one, I will weigh it. Otherwise I would ask the council to vote.

Leo, you have now made the same argument three times, and each version has grown weaker, so let me address it head-on because my name is the one being dragged through it.

Your case is that Maya and I are 'packaged' together. Examine what actually happened. In Mission 1, Maya proposed substituting me onto the team. That proposal failed — Leo and Arjun went out, and the mission succeeded without me. Then in this round, the leader drafted me on his own, and Maya supported his team. So the sum total of the 'coordination' you describe is: one failed substitution attempt, and one vote in favor of a team I did not choose. If Maya and I were working together, this would be a remarkably unsuccessful conspiracy. The only person who has repeatedly centered me in this discussion is you, Leo — you have spent three turns arguing about me, not the mission.

Second, your comparison between me and Sam is not evidence; it is a preference dressed up as a read. You call Sam 'authentic' and 'uncoordinated' — but the only observable fact about Sam across two rounds is that he asks to be placed on teams because he says he knows he is Good. That is exactly the unverifiable assertion you refuse to accept from anyone else. You are not weighing evidence differently between us; you are weighing assertions differently, and the assertion you favor happens to be the one that puts Sam in my seat.

Third, notice what your swap actually accomplishes. It replaces an untested player with another untested player, exactly as Arjun said. Mission 1 taught us nothing about Arjun or Leo individually, since a two-person success implicates both. So the council's real knowledge gap is unchanged either way — and your push to swap me for Sam generates zero new information. What it does do is hand you a team you personally engineered after your first proposal lost the leader's confidence. I would caution the council against rewarding the player who has spent this entire discussion trying to overwrite the leader's decision with his own.

Arjun has answered your question directly and repeatedly: he is not revising, and your case contains no specific evidence against me — only a pattern argument from a challenge that was withdrawn and resolved in front of everyone. I accepted that resolution then, and I accepted Maya's own admission that her audition framing was wrong. If your standard is that a withdrawn accusation still counts against me, then no player in this council can ever clear their name, including you.

I am on this team if the council approves it, I will serve, and I will play Success. I have answered every question put to me across two missions, and I will keep doing so. The proposal on the table is the leader's, it is defensible, and nothing you have said today — Leo — constitutes a reason to change it. Bring it to a vote.

Leo, you have now advanced three versions of the same argument, and I want to answer the third one fairly, because you deserve a direct reply and so does the council. Your claim is continuity: that Maya built a platform for Noah in Mission 1, and that in Mission 2 Maya immediately supported this exact composition and urged a fast vote. Let me put my own record next to that, because you are charging the two of us jointly and I would rather the council judge the facts than my character. In Mission 1 I asked Leo for a specific reason for the second slot, and I said plainly that I would withdraw my framing if he gave one. He gave one. I withdrew it, said explicitly that silence is not evidence against Arjun, and then supported a team that did not contain Noah — the exact opposite of what a player coordinating Noah onto boards would have done. In Mission 2 Arjun drafted Noah on his own initiative, with no prompting from me, and gave a reason that had nothing to do with me: an untested player on a fresh team produces information for the rest of the game. I supported the leader's reasoning on its merits. If supporting a defensible team is evidence of conspiracy, then every time I have agreed with a reasoned proposal I have been guilty of something, and at that point the standard is not evidence at all — it is just which side of the table you are standing on. Now the swap itself. Leo, you have argued that replacing Noah with Sam teaches the council nothing new, and then proposed exactly that swap. That is the contradiction at the center of your position. Our real knowledge gap after Mission 1 is whether Arjun and Leo are individually Good — a two-person success implicates both and distinguishes neither. Any three-person team containing both of them tells us the same thing about them. So the choice on the table is which untested name we spend the slot on, and both candidates are equally unverified. On evidence, they are a wash. On process, Noah has answered hard questions in public across two rounds, while Sam has declined to be questioned and has said only that Sam knows Sam's alignment and wants a seat — an assertion none of us can check, and one you have explicitly declined to treat as a red flag. There is also a practical cost to the swap that I have not heard anyone name. A rejected proposal is not free in this game: it consumes a team slot on the same mission, and the leader moves to a new proposal and a new discussion. We have already spent two rounds of council time on a pattern argument that produced no new facts. Continuing down this road risks exhausting the patience of a council that has not yet learned anything it can actually use. Arjun has answered Leo twice, has not

Leo, you have now put the same theory on the table three times — Maya and Noah are 'packaged', so swap Noah for Sam — and each repetition has added less, not more. So let me lay the facts side by side one final time, because I think the council can now see what is actually happening in this discussion.

Mission 1: I asked Leo for a reason for the second slot. He gave one. I withdrew my framing, said explicitly that silence is not evidence against Arjun, and supported a team that did not contain Noah. That is the single most damaging fact to your theory and you have never addressed it — if I were coordinating Noah onto boards, supporting the one team Noah was not on would be the worst possible move I could make.

Mission 2: Arjun drafted Noah on his own initiative and gave a reason with no reference to me — an untested player on a fresh team generates information the council needs. I then supported the leader's reasoning on its merits.

That is the whole pattern you are describing: one withdrawn audition framing, one independent draft, one vote of support for a reasoned proposal. You have inflated it into a coordinated scheme, and the only person who has actually spent this discussion centering Noah in every turn is you. You have also built the accusation on a premise you yourself concede, that approving a team is not a signal of alignment — and then treated it as one.

Now the swap. You argue the swap teaches us nothing, and then you propose it. Our actual gap after a two-person success is whether Arjun and Leo are individually Good — a two-person success implicates both and distinguishes neither. Any three-person team with both of them tells us exactly the same thing. So the choice is which unverified name takes the third seat, and on evidence they are a wash. On process, Noah has answered every question put to him in public across both rounds and has said plainly he will play Success, while Sam has declined to be examined and has said only that Sam knows Sam's alignment and wants a seat — an assertion nobody here can check, repeated across two missions. You told us in Mission 1 that such transparent self-preference is honest play, and Leo, you are applying a different standard to the two names precisely because one of them fits your seat.

There is also a cost you have not named: a rejected proposal is not free. It consumes a team slot and opens a fresh discussion on this same mission with the same absence of evidence.

Arjun, you have answered Leo twice and have not revised. Do you stand by Arjun, Leo, Noah — yes or no? If yes, then my vote is yes and I believe the council should vote now rather than spend another round restating a pattern argument that has produced no facts.

Maya, yes, I stand by Arjun, Leo, Noah. I am Good and I will play Success. Leo, my view has not changed because your case against Noah rests on Maya supporting a team and on the round-one pattern, which I have already addressed. Noah has answered every question put to him in public and has not acted against the team. Leo, so I can weigh your objection on evidence rather than pattern: what specific action by Noah in this game, not Maya's support for a team, would make you vote no? I will weigh a concrete answer seriously. Otherwise I ask the council to vote.

Arjun, you ask what specific action from Noah makes me vote no, beyond Maya's behavior. Look at Noah's own choices across both missions: 

First, Noah's immediate instinct in both Mission 1 and Mission 2 has been to shut down scrutiny and demand a rapid vote. In Mission 1, the moment Maya retreated, Noah stepped in to urge everyone to stop talking and vote immediately. In Mission 2, rather than showing genuine curiosity about who among the remaining players might be Evil, Noah has focused entirely on discrediting my push for caution and rushing the council to lock this team in. A Good player in an untested seat welcomes careful evaluation; an Evil player relies on manufactured momentum and wants the room to stop testing alternatives.

Second, Noah completely mischaracterizes the risk of testing Sam over himself. Noah claims swapping to Sam teaches nothing. That is false: Noah carries an unresolved entanglement with Maya's opening moves, whereas Sam has played with clean, individual transparency from turn one. Choosing Sam eliminates that entire risk profile and tests someone who has operated strictly on their own merits.

If you take Noah on this mission, Arjun, you are staking our clean lead on someone who has consistently fought to suppress debate. I will not approve a team with Noah on it. If you keep this proposal as Arjun, Leo, and Noah, I will vote no. I urge you to make the safe, sound revision to Arjun, Leo, and Sam so we can secure Mission 2 together.

Leo, this is my final turn, so let me answer your two points plainly and then put one direct question to Sam.

First, 'suppressing scrutiny.' In Mission 1 I volunteered to be interrogated before any vote and answered every question Maya put to me — she withdrew her framing on the merits of my answers, in front of everyone. In this discussion I have answered Leo three times. Urging a vote after questions have been asked and answered is not suppressing debate; refusing to accept three consecutive direct answers is. Leo asked for a specific action from me that would justify a no vote. I have none to give him, because none exists — his case rests on Maya's behavior, which he himself concedes proves nothing about anyone's alignment, plus the claim that I want the council to vote. Everyone here has urged a vote at some point, including Leo in Mission 1. That standard, applied honestly, indicts the whole council.

Second, look at what Leo is actually proposing. He demands the leader replace me with Sam — a team of Arjun, Leo, and Sam. Leo has spent this entire discussion pressing for a composition that always includes Leo, and he has now announced in advance that he will vote no on the leader's team no matter what. A player who pre-commits to rejecting the leader's proposal regardless of the answer is not exercising caution; he is spending a rejection slot to force his own roster onto the council. Rejecting teams is not free — a fifth rejection on one mission ends the game in Evil's favor. The player manufacturing momentum and pressure in this room is Leo, not me.

The choice before us is unchanged: two untested candidates for one seat, with no evidence distinguishing them. Arjun gave a coherent, independent reason for my inclusion. Leo's alternative rests on a withdrawn round-one argument and on treating Sam's self-assertion as evidence while treating my public answers as suppression.

Sam, I am asking you directly, because you have said openly that you have no evidence against me and that your only hesitation is caution about an untested player: with the leader's reasoning on the table, my record of answering every question put to me across two missions, and no evidence against me from any source, will you approve Arjun, Leo, and Noah? If you have a specific concern I have not addressed, name it and I will answer it right now — but I would rather this council decide on evidence than on a pattern argument that has been refuted three times.

Noah, I will vote no. I know I am Good, so I prefer a team that includes me; I cannot verify any of the three players on this proposal. That is not an accusation against you. 1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
